name: STM32G0B1RET6
title: STM32G0B1xB/xC/xE Arm Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers, 64 MHz, 128 to 512 Kbytes Flash, 144 Kbytes SRAM, USB, UCPD, FDCAN, 1.7 V to 3.6 V
summary: A mainstream Cortex-M0+ microcontroller line running at up to 64 MHz from a 1.7 V to 3.6 V supply, with 128, 256 or 512 Kbytes of dual-bank ECC Flash and 144 Kbytes of SRAM (128 Kbytes when parity is used). It carries a crystal-less full-speed USB device and host, two USB Type-C Power Delivery controllers, two FDCANs, six USARTs, two LPUARTs, three I2Cs, three SPIs (two with I2S), a 12-bit 2.5 MSps ADC, a two-channel 12-bit DAC, three comparators, fifteen timers and a calendar RTC on VBAT, in packages of 32 to 100 pins with a separate VDDIO2 I/O supply on most. STM32G0B1CBT6 is the 128 Kbyte LQFP48 part for -40 °C to 85 °C ambient, with 44 GPIOs.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M0+ with MPU, up to 64 MHz
128, 256 or 512 Kbytes Flash (ECC, two banks), 144 Kbytes SRAM (128 Kbytes parity-checked)
VDD 1.7 V to 3.6 V; VDDIO2 1.6 V to 3.6 V; VBAT 1.55 V to 3.6 V
8.6 mA typ at 64 MHz from Flash, Range 1, 25 °C, VDD = 3.0 V
3.3 µA / 0.2 µA / 38 nA typ at 3 V, 25 °C, RTC off
12-bit, 2.5 MSps, up to 16 external channels, 16-bit by oversampling
two 12-bit channels, buffered or not, with sample-and-hold
full-speed device and host, crystal-less with HSI48 and clock recovery
HSI16 15.88 to 16.08 MHz at 3 V, 30 °C; HSI48 48 MHz; LSI 32 kHz
-40 °C to 85 °C, 105 °C or 125 °C ambient by order code

rows: LQFP48: STM32G0B1 CET6; UFQFPN48: STM32G0B1 CEU6
notes: An order code adds the package letter, the temperature digit (6: -40 to 85 °C, 7: -40 to 105 °C, 3: -40 to 125 °C) and options: STM32G0B1CBT6 is the 128 Kbyte LQFP48 part for -40 °C to 85 °C.
The 32-, 48- and 64-pin parts come as a GP version and an N version (N after the temperature digit); the N version trades I/Os for a VDDIO2 pin, and on 48 and 64 pins also a second VSS.

circuits.title: Power supply scheme
circuits.description: Each supply pin gets ceramic decoupling at the pin: VDD/VDDA takes one 100 nF and one 4.7 µF to VSS/VSSA, VDDIO2 takes 100 nF plus 4.7 µF, and VREF+ takes 100 nF with an optional 1 µF. A 1.55 V to 3.6 V source on VBAT keeps the backup domain (LSE, RTC, backup registers) alive through the internal power switch when VDD is gone.
notes: Where the package lacks a VBAT or VREF+ pin, that pad is bonded to VDD/VDDA inside; where it lacks VDDIO2, those I/Os run from VDD.
The capacitors sit as close as possible to their pins, or under them on the back of the board.

circuits.title: 8 MHz crystal on the HSE oscillator
circuits.description: An 8 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator across OSC_IN and OSC_OUT, with a load capacitor from each side to ground; the 200 kΩ feedback resistor is inside the part. REXT, in series between the crystal and OSC_OUT, is sized for the crystal. CL1 and CL2 are ceramic parts of 5 pF to 20 pF for high-frequency use, normally equal; the crystal's rated load is their series value, counting about 10 pF of pin and board capacitance.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors takes the place of Y1, C1 and C2.
Crystal and capacitors go as near the oscillator pins as they can.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal on the LSE oscillator
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal across OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT with a load capacitor from each pin to ground; the drive strength is chosen in software with LSEDRV. No resistor goes across the crystal: none is needed, and fitting one is not allowed.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors takes the place of Y1, C1 and C2.
Crystal and capacitors go as near the oscillator pins as they can.

circuits.title: NRST pin protection
circuits.description: A 0.1 µF capacitor from NRST to ground, close to the part, guards against stray resets, and a push-button to ground resets by hand; the pull-up RPU is inside. Whatever drives NRST must bring it below VIL(NRST) max, or the reset is missed.

circuits.title: ADC input connection
circuits.description: A source VAIN drives an analog input through its own resistance RAIN; board and pad add a parasitic capacitance to ground. RAIN stays within the limit for the chosen resolution and sampling time (50 kΩ at most). A large parasitic capacitance costs accuracy, which a slower ADC clock wins back.

operation.text: Arm Cortex-M0+ at up to 64 MHz: a two-stage pipeline on a Von Neumann bus with a single-cycle multiplier. A memory protection unit lets an RTOS keep each task out of the memory of the others; it may be left unused.

Up to 512 Kbytes in two banks, readable while the other is written, with ECC that corrects one bit, flags two, and keeps the failing address in a register. Option bytes set the protections: readout protection Level 0 (none), Level 1 (no Flash access while debug is connected or the part boots from RAM or the bootloader) and Level 2 (debug, RAM boot and bootloader turned off for good); write protection of two areas per bank in 2 Kbyte steps; and PCROP, an execute-only area that only CPU instruction fetches reach, with an option bit deciding whether it is wiped when RDP drops from Level 1 to Level 0.

Part of the Flash can be locked away after it has run: setting SEC_PROT (writable once) closes that area so nothing reaches it until the next system reset. It suits boot code meant to run once and keep its secrets from the application.
128 Kbytes with hardware parity, at CPU speed with no wait states. Where parity is not wanted its bits serve as more memory, giving 144 Kbytes.

The boot pin, a GPIO enabled by the boot selector option bit, and the option bits choose boot from user Flash, system memory or SRAM. The system-memory bootloader reprograms the Flash over USART (PA9/PA10, PC10/PC11 or PA2/PA3), I2C (PB6/PB7 or PB10/PB11), SPI (PA4 to PA7 or PB12 to PB15), USB (PA11/PA12) or FDCAN (PD0/PD1).

Computes a CRC with a programmable polynomial and size, for checking transmitted or stored data; under EN/IEC 60335-1 it can check the Flash contents at run time against a signature made at link time.

VDD, 1.7 V to 3.6 V on the VDD/VDDA pin, feeds the regulator, reset, power management and clocks; 1.7 V is the highest VPOR, and once reset has released the part works down to VPDR min. VDDA comes from the same pin and must be at least 1.62 V for the ADC and comparators, 1.8 V for the DAC and 2.4 V for VREFBUF. VDDIO1 equals VDD. VDDIO2, 1.6 V to 3.6 V on its own pin, powers a group of I/Os and must not be applied without a valid VDD. VBAT, 1.55 V to 3.6 V, keeps the RTC, TAMP, LSE and backup registers running through a switch when VDD is absent; where the package has no VBAT pin it is bonded to VDD/VDDA. VCORE comes from the internal regulator and feeds the logic, SRAM and Flash (the Flash also takes VDD).

VREF+ is the reference input of the analog blocks, or the VREFBUF output when the buffer runs. Below VDDA = 2 V it must equal VDDA; at or above 2 V it lies between 2 V and VDDA. It may be grounded while no analog block that uses it is on. VREFBUF gives about 2.048 V (VDDA at least 2.4 V) or about 2.5 V (VDDA at least 2.8 V), chosen by the VRS bit. On packages with no VREF+ pin it is tied to VDD inside and VREFBUF must stay off.

A power-on/power-down reset, active in every mode but Shutdown, holds the part in reset below VPOR/PDR with no external reset part. A brownout reset with four rising and four falling thresholds is set in the option bytes. A software-enabled programmable voltage detector compares VDD with VPVD and interrupts on a falling, rising or either crossing.

Run and Sleep use the main regulator; Stop and both low-power modes use the low-power regulator. In Standby and Shutdown both are off with their outputs high-impedance, except that in Standby the low-power regulator can stay on to keep the SRAM alone.

Run follows any reset. Sleep stops only the CPU; peripherals run and wake it. Low-power run takes VCORE from the low-power regulator with the CPU at 2 MHz or less, code in SRAM or Flash; Low-power sleep is entered from it and stops the CPU clock. Stop 0 and Stop 1 keep SRAM and registers, stop all VCORE clocks and turn off the PLL, HSI16 and HSE while LSE or LSI run on and the RTC may stay active; some wakeup peripherals may start HSI16 to handle the event; the main regulator stays on in Stop 0 and is off in Stop 1. Standby turns the main regulator off, POR/PDR stays on, the low-power regulator may keep the SRAM, each I/O may keep a pull-up or pull-down, and only RTC-domain and standby registers survive; it ends on NRST, IWDG, a WKUP pin edge, an RTC event or an LSE clock failure. Shutdown also stops LSI and has no BOR or supply monitoring, so the RTC domain cannot change over to VBAT; SRAM and registers outside the RTC domain are lost; it ends on NRST, IWDG, a WKUP pin edge or an RTC event.
While reset is held and as it ends, the I/O Schmitt triggers are off to save current, and when the reset comes from inside the part the NRST pull-up is disconnected.

The VBAT domain holds the RTC, LSE and backup registers and draws very little. A battery or supercapacitor on VBAT keeps it running; an internal supervisor switches the domain between VDD and VBAT, taking VDD whenever both are valid. While VDD is valid an internal charger can charge the cell on VBAT. In VBAT mode no external interrupt or RTC event can bring the part out, since VDD is not valid.

SYSCLK comes from the 4 to 48 MHz HSE crystal or resonator oscillator (or an external clock in bypass), the 16 MHz HSI16 RC (trimmable), or the PLL (64 MHz max) fed from HSE or HSI16. The RTC has the 32.768 kHz LSE (four drive levels, or bypass) or the 32 kHz LSI (±5 %), which also clocks the IWDG. I2S, USARTs, I2Cs, LPTIMs, ADC and USB can each take their own kernel clock. The clock security system switches SYSCLK to HSI16 on an HSE failure and can interrupt; an LSE failure can also interrupt. MCO puts an internal clock on a pin; LSCO puts LSI or LSE out in every low-power mode except VBAT. AHB and APB run at 64 MHz at most.

Software makes each pin an output (push-pull or open-drain), an input (pull-up, pull-down or neither), or an alternate function; most also carry digital or analog extras. A locking sequence freezes the configuration against stray writes.

A 12-channel single-AHB-master DMA moves data between peripherals and memories in any direction, with four software priority levels per channel (lower channel number wins a tie), independent source and destination widths, circular buffers, transfers of 0 to 2^16 - 1 items, and an interrupt per channel on complete, half or error. The DMAMUX routes any request line to any channel, optionally synchronised to an event, and can generate requests from trigger inputs.

The NVIC has 4 priority levels, an NMI, 32 maskable lines and 10 core exceptions, with hardware stacking, tail-chaining and late arrival. The EXTI has edge-detecting channels for any GPIO and some peripheral signals, each maskable, catches pulses shorter than its clock period, and latches events in Stop mode to show what woke the part.

A 12-bit SAR ADC, extended to 16 bits by hardware oversampling of up to 256 samples, with up to 16 external channels and three internal ones (temperature sensor, VREFINT, VBAT/3). Single or scan conversions, DMA service, an analog watchdog on one, several or all channels, timer triggers, and an auto-off that powers it only while converting. Its clock is independent of the CPU, so it samples at about 2 MSps even with a slow core. It works over the whole VDD range.

The sensor's output VTS rises linearly with temperature and is wired to an ADC input; its offset differs part to part, so without calibration it only suits relative readings. Each part carries factory readings at 30 °C and 130 °C (TS_CAL1, TS_CAL2) and a VREFINT reading at 30 °C, all taken at VDDA = VREF+ = 3.0 V and held read-only in the engineering bytes. VBAT is read through an internal divide-by-3 bridge, since it may exceed VDDA.

Two 12-bit buffered channels, each a resistor string and inverting amplifier, sharing one digital block: 8- or 12-bit data, left or right alignment, factory and user offset trim of the buffer, synchronised update, noise and triangle generation, independent or simultaneous conversion, DMA per channel, timer and external triggers, and a low-power sample-and-hold with an internal or external capacitor.

When on, the buffer drives 2.048 V or 2.5 V onto VREF+ for the analog blocks and outside parts; when off, an external reference may drive VREF+. Packages that bond VREF+ to VDD/VDDA cannot use the buffer.

Three rail-to-rail comparators with programmable hysteresis, speed and output polarity. The reference is an I/O, a DAC channel, VREFINT or 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 of it. They wake the part from Stop, interrupt, break or trigger timers, and pair up as a window comparator.

TIM1 is a 16-bit advanced timer at up to 128 MHz with four channels, three complementary outputs with programmable dead time, edge or centre-aligned PWM and one-pulse mode; in debug its counter can freeze with the outputs off. TIM2 (32-bit), TIM3 and TIM4 (16-bit) have four channels, encoder inputs, DMA and up/down counting. TIM14 has one channel; TIM15 (up to 128 MHz) two channels and one complementary; TIM16 and TIM17 one channel and one complementary. All link for synchronisation or chaining. TIM6 and TIM7 are basic timebases, chiefly for DAC triggers. LPTIM1 and LPTIM2 are 16-bit with compare, PWM or pulse output, one-shot or continuous, encoder mode and a glitch filter, clocked from LSE, LSI, HSI16, APB or an external input that counts with no internal clock; on LSE, LSI or external clock they run through Stop and wake the part.

The IWDG is an 8-bit prescaler and 12-bit downcounter with a refresh window, on the LSI, working in Stop and Standby and started by hardware or software as the option bytes choose. The WWDG is a 7-bit downcounter on the system clock with an early-warning interrupt. Both counters can freeze in debug. SysTick is a 24-bit auto-reload downcounter with an interrupt at zero and a selectable clock.

A BCD calendar with subseconds and automatic month lengths and leap years, a programmable alarm, shift correction of 1 to 32767 clock pulses, 50 or 60 Hz reference input, digital calibration in 0.95 ppm steps, two tamper pins with filters, a timestamp on a pin, a tamper or the change to VBAT, and a 17-bit wakeup timer. It runs from LSE (in VBAT and every low-power mode), LSI (every low-power mode but Shutdown, not VBAT) or HSE/32. Every RTC event can interrupt and wake the part. Five 32-bit backup registers (20 bytes) survive a VDD loss with VBAT valid, and are not cleared by system or power reset or by waking from Standby or Shutdown.

Three I2C controllers to rev. 5 of the bus specification: master, slave and multimaster at 100 kbit/s, 400 kbit/s and 1 Mbit/s (Fast-mode Plus with stronger I/Os), 7- and 10-bit addresses, programmable setup and hold, clock stretching, analog and digital filters and a one-byte DMA buffer. I2C1 and I2C2 add SMBus 3.0 (PEC, ARP, alert, timeouts) and PMBus 1.3, an independent kernel clock and wakeup from Stop on an address match.

Six USARTs at up to 8 Mbit/s with CTS/RTS and RS485 driver enable, multiprocessor, synchronous master and single-wire half-duplex modes, all with DMA. USART1 to USART3 add smartcard, IrDA, LIN, auto baud rate, receiver timeout, Modbus and an independent kernel clock with wakeup from Stop on a start bit, any frame or a chosen frame. Two LPUARTs do the same Stop-mode wakeup at minimum current: from the 32.768 kHz LSE alone they reach 9600 baud, faster with a faster clock.

Three SPIs at up to 32 Mbit/s master or slave, full or half duplex or simplex, 4- to 16-bit frames, eight master clock rates from a 3-bit prescaler, NSS pulse and TI modes, hardware CRC and DMA. SPI1 and SPI2 also run as I2S, master or slave, half duplex, four audio standards, 16-, 24- or 32-bit frames, 8 kHz to 192 kHz sampling from an 8-bit prescaler, and a master clock out at 256 times the sample rate.

A full-speed (12 Mbit/s) USB 2.0 device and host controller with its own PHY, an internal DP pull-up, battery charging detection to BCD rev. 1.2, Link Power Management, up to 1 Kbyte of packet memory and suspend/resume. It needs an exact 48 MHz clock: from the PLL with an HSE crystal, or from HSI48 trimmed automatically from the bus SOF packets, which needs no crystal.

UCPD1 and UCPD2 meet USB Type-C rev. 1.2 and USB PD rev. 3.0. Their dedicated I/Os carry Rp (every value) and Rd terminations, dead-battery support, PD message transmit and receive and fast role swap. The logic debounces Type-C levels, detects FRS, moves PD payload byte by byte with DMA, and does the PD timing, CRC, 4b5b coding, ordered sets and preamble clock recovery. It keeps listening for PD messages and FRS in Stop mode.
Two CAN modules to ISO 11898-1 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and CAN FD 1.0, each with 1 Kbyte of message RAM for filters, receive FIFOs and buffers, transmit event FIFOs and transmit buffers.
An Arm serial wire debug port (SWDIO, SWCLK) connects a debugger.

Voltages are referred to VSS. Min and max figures hold over the worst case of temperature, supply and clock, tested on every part at TA = 25 °C and TA(max); figures marked as characterization or design are not production tested, and characterization limits are mean ±3σ. Typical figures are at TA = 25 °C and VDD = VDDA = VDDIO2 = 3 V and are guidance only, as are the typical curves. Pin figures use a 50 pF load.

Supply currents are taken with every I/O in analog mode, every peripheral off unless named, the fewest Flash wait states for fHCLK (RM0444), and fPCLK = fHCLK whenever peripherals run. IDD flows into VDD/VDDA (and VDDIO2); IDDVBAT into VBAT.

VDD/VDDA, VDDIO2 and VREF+ each need ceramic decoupling to VSS/VSSA (100 nF plus 4.7 µF on VDD/VDDA and on VDDIO2; 100 nF, and optionally 1 µF, on VREF+), mounted as near the pins as possible or right under them on the back of the board. The 100 nF part should be a good ceramic at the chip.

An input with pull-up draws current whenever something outside holds it low, set by the pull resistor values. An input sitting at a mid-level voltage draws current through its Schmitt trigger; a floating input can drift there or toggle from noise. Pins not in use, and ADC inputs, go to analog mode, or are held at a firm level by a pull resistor or by making them outputs.

A GPIO sinks or sources up to ±8 mA at the rated VOL/VOH, and up to ±15 mA with relaxed levels. The current all I/Os on VDDIO1 source, plus the core's own draw, must stay inside IVDD; the current all I/Os sink, plus the core's, inside IVSS.

These three pins hang on the backup power switch, which sinks only 3 mA: as outputs they are limited to 2 MHz into 30 pF and must not source current. After the RTC domain powers up they are GPIOs, and their use then follows the RTC registers, which a system reset leaves alone.

SYSCFG_CFGR1 can bring PA9 and PA10 out on the PA11 and PA12 pins in place of the default. PA13 (SWDIO) and PA14 (SWCLK, shared with BOOT0) come out of reset as debug pins with an internal pull-up on PA13 and pull-down on PA14.

NRST is a CMOS input with a permanent pull-up RPU (25 kΩ to 55 kΩ). Pulses under 70 ns are filtered out and pulses over 350 ns always reset. On PF2-NRST packages the pin can instead serve as GPIO PF2.
Below VDDA = 2.4 V the I/O analog switches need the booster on (BOOSTEN in SYSCFG_CFGR1) for the ADC figures to hold; at or above 2.4 V it stays off. It starts in 240 µs and draws up to 900 µA.

Calibrate the ADC after each power-up. Negative injection on one analog pin degrades conversions on the others; a Schottky diode to ground on pins that may see it is advised. Keep the source resistance under the RAIN limit for the sampling time, keep board capacitance on the input small or slow the ADC clock, and decouple VDD/VDDA with a good 100 nF ceramic at the chip.

SDA and SCL are not true open-drain: in open-drain mode the PMOS to VDDIO1 is switched off but still there. Only FT_f pins meet the Fm+ sink current. Every SDA and SCL pin has an analog spike filter of 50 ns to 260 ns.

PA11 is USB_DM and PA12 USB_DP; the DP pull-up and the driver's matching impedance are inside, so no series resistors are needed. The full-speed figures hold from VDD = 3.0 V; the transceiver works down to 2.7 V with degraded characteristics. With VBUS sensing on, PA9 stays a floating input and the sensing draws about 200 µA through it.

UCPD1 uses CC1 on PA8 and CC2 on PB15, with dead-battery pins DBCC1 on PA9 and DBCC2 on PA10; UCPD2 uses CC1 on PD0 and CC2 on PD2, with DBCC1 on PD1 and DBCC2 on PD3. As a sink only, VDD may be 3.0 V to 3.6 V; as sink and source it must be 3.135 V to 3.465 V.

EMC is characterised at component level with simple software, and the result in an application depends heavily on its software. Handle runaway conditions (corrupted program counter, unexpected reset, corrupted control registers) in the software. Most failures can be reproduced by holding NRST or an oscillator pin low for 1 second, or by applying ESD to the part (application note AN1015).

Each temperature digit guarantees an ambient at full dissipation and a maximum junction temperature (6: 85 °C / 105 °C; 7: 105 °C / 125 °C; 3: 125 °C / 130 °C). Since a part rarely runs at full power, work out the real dissipation and junction temperature with the thermal resistance of the package (JESD51-2, still air) and pick the digit from that.

The top side carries the product identification, a date code (year and week), a revision code and a pin 1 (or ball A1) mark; markings vary with the supply chain. Parts marked ES or E, or shipped with an engineering-sample notice, are not qualified for production.

The 32-, 48- and 64-pin parts come in a GP version and an N version (an N after the temperature digit in the order code). The N version gives up a few I/Os for a VDDIO2 supply pin (and, on 48 and 64 pins, an extra VSS), and has two UCPD ports where the GP version has one; on the GP 32-pin part that one port has a single CC line.
